name: ザ ガーデンラウンジ (The Garden Lounge)

claims.text: The kitchen runs French-style courses with bread, pastry, and sauced mains — significant wheat cross-contamination risk in a non-dedicated kitchen. No dedicated GF preparation area confirmed.
No wheat-free soy sauce confirmed. Standard Japanese soy sauce (containing wheat) is likely used in any Japanese-style preparations on the menu.
Vegan requests require advance notice at reservation. The kitchen routinely uses dairy and egg in French-style courses, so cross-contact risk exists without explicit kitchen communication.

The restaurant requests that guests disclose all food allergies before arrival, noting that post-arrival requests may not be accommodated. Even with advance notice, the venue reserves the right to decline accommodation if guest safety cannot be assured.
Allergy information is formally collected at reservation stage, and the reservation platforms (ikyu, TableCheck) list vegan (egg/dairy-free) as an available accommodation category.

name: ザ・カワブン・ナゴヤ (The Kawabun Nagoya)

claims.text: Italian courses feature fresh pasta and wheat-based preparations; no separate gluten-free cooking line or dedicated equipment has been documented.
Italian kitchen is unlikely to rely on wheat-containing soy sauce, but dressings, sauces, and desserts may contain wheat; no ingredient list is publicly available.
Courses are built around meat, seafood, and dairy; shared kitchen surfaces and cookware make vegan cross-contact likely without prior arrangement.
The Kenzo Estate partner listing notes the restaurant can accommodate guests with food restrictions and international guests, but no formal allergy protocol is documented publicly.
Course-based dining with advance reservations creates an opportunity to communicate dietary needs directly with the kitchen before arrival.

name: 鳥開総本家 金シャチ横丁店 (Torikai Sohonke Kinshachi Yokocho)

claims.text: Tebasaki (fried chicken wings) are coated and deep-fried. No dedicated fryer for any allergen-free preparation is documented. Cross-contamination with wheat from frying is a realistic risk.

The cooking philosophy page confirms the use of 'Central Japan soy sauce marinade' (中日本しょうゆダレ) in the karaage and wing preparations. Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat; no tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere on the official site or third-party sources.
The entire menu is built on chicken and chicken-derived ingredients (egg, bonito dashi). There is no plant-based preparation at this restaurant; vegan cross-contact is unavoidable throughout.

No allergen declaration, staff allergy protocol, or dietary accommodation program is documented on the official site, Tabelog listing, Kinshachi Yokocho operator page, or any third-party source reviewed. Diners with serious allergies should contact the restaurant directly before visiting.

name: トラットリア ドン・アントニオ (Trattoria DON-ANTONIO)

claims.text: No information on dedicated GF fryer or separate cooking surfaces. This is a pasta-and-pizza kitchen where wheat flour is in constant use — cross-contamination risk should be assumed high.
No soy sauce noted in menu descriptions; this is Italian cuisine so soy sauce is not expected. Wheat risk comes from pasta dough, pizza crust, and possible flour-dusted prep surfaces.
Standard Italian trattoria kitchen — butter, dairy, eggs, and meat stocks are routine. No vegan-safe prep protocols mentioned anywhere.
The Italian owner speaks fluent Japanese and is known for personal, attentive service; direct communication about dietary needs should be feasible. No formal allergy protocol is documented.
Owner Antonio's fluent Japanese and warm, table-side manner make it easier than at many restaurants to explain dietary needs directly to the person who runs the kitchen.

name: トラットリア タピーロ (Trattoria TAPIRO)

claims.text: The kitchen is built around stone-oven pizza and handmade pasta — both wheat-intensive — making flour airborne cross-contamination a near-certainty. No source mentions any GF protocol.
No mention of soy sauce use in any reviewed source, but standard Italian kitchen soy-sauce risk is low; primary wheat risk is from pizza dough and pasta throughout the kitchen.
Cheese and meat are core to almost every menu item; shared prep surfaces and ovens make vegan cross-contact likely.

No allergy handling policy, allergen menu, or accommodation language was found on any platform reviewed. Diners with serious allergies should contact the restaurant directly at 052-325-3699 before visiting.
Cards, e-money, and QR payments accepted — no cash-only barrier for international visitors.
Online reservations available and same-day bookings accepted until 21:00, reducing uncertainty for group visits.

name: 鰻のうな文 本店 (Unabun (Unagi no Unabun Honten))

claims.text: No allergen information is published. Traditional kabayaki tare contains wheat-based soy sauce applied to all eel dishes; no wheat-free alternative is mentioned anywhere.
Shared cooking surfaces (charcoal grill) and communal tare pot are standard at this style of eel restaurant, creating cross-contamination risk.
Kabayaki sauce (tare) is the defining flavour element of all unagi dishes here; standard Japanese tare is made with wheat-containing soy sauce and mirin. No wheat-free soy sauce option is listed.
The entire menu is eel-based. There are no plant-based dishes, so vegan cross-contact is a moot point — the restaurant is simply not suitable for vegans.
No allergy-handling policy or dedicated procedure is listed on any platform. Contact the restaurant directly (052-971-3148) well in advance if you have a wheat allergy.
Completely non-smoking interior; small, consistent kitchen focused on a single ingredient, which limits the variety of allergen sources present.

Traditional unagi tare (kabayaki glaze) is made with standard wheat-containing soy sauce. No GF alternative is offered or advertised. Cross-contamination from shared grilling surfaces and kitchen equipment must be assumed.

The signature tare — built up over generations from standard Japanese soy sauce (which contains wheat) — is central to every eel dish on the menu. There is no wheat-free soy sauce option indicated anywhere.
The entire menu is eel-based; fish dashi is used in all soups. No plant-based cooking surfaces or utensils are separated. Not applicable for vegan diners.
No allergy handling policy is published on the official site or Tabelog. Reservations are phone-only; calling ahead at 052-951-8781 is the only way to discuss dietary needs before visiting.
Eel is prepared fresh to order (approximately 20–40 minutes), meaning there is no pre-made batch sitting with mixed ingredients — though the tare itself remains a fixed wheat source.

name: ウッタムカレー 丸の内店 (Uttam Curry Marunouchi)

claims.text: Naan is wheat-based and baked in a shared tandoor oven used for all breads and tandoori items; no separate GF baking surface or protocol is mentioned anywhere.

No soy sauce is listed in the menu descriptions; Indian and Nepalese curry recipes at this restaurant do not appear to use soy sauce, but no allergen statement is published and kitchen practices are unconfirmed.
Dairy (ghee/butter) is used in naan and likely in tandoori dishes; the tandoor oven is shared. Vegan curries are not labeled as prepared separately from dairy-containing items.

No allergen menu, allergy protocol, or dietary accommodation procedure is published. One reviewer noted some language barrier with staff. Phone inquiry (052-202-0177) before visiting is advised for any serious dietary restriction.

Multiple vegetable curries are available daily — vegetable curry, chickpea masala, bean curry, spinach-potato, and eggplant dry curry — giving plant-based diners real choices without relying on meat-free adaptations.
Rice is available as a substitute for naan at no stated extra charge, providing a wheat-free carb option if the curry sauce itself is flour-free.
